claims.text: A hybrid framework will combine ab initio defect and impurity-scattering calculations with machine-learning regression trained on experimental conductivity data.
The hybrid framework will significantly improve conductivity-prediction accuracy relative to conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The framework can predict temperature-dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr with realistic defect concentrations.
The framework is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr specimens both with and without 1 wt.% oxygen.
Explicit defect density and oxygen-scattering parameters, including scattering cross-sections and electron-phonon-coupling modifications, influence electron mean free paths.
Impurity- and defect-induced states dominate conductivity behavior from approximately 0 to 200 K.
Thermal activation effects become significant from approximately 300 to 1200 K.
Defects and oxygen impurities create additional electron-scattering centers.
The additional scattering centers reduce effective charge-carrier mobility and alter electrical conductivity.
Combining microscopic scattering calculations with machine-learning refinement bridges the gap between idealized crystal models and real HfNbTaTiZr behavior.
The framework will predict conductivity within ±15% of experimental measurements in both specified temperature regimes.
Perfect-crystal analytical models deviate more substantially from the measurements than the proposed framework.
The approach is valid only in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
Phenomena outside the specified temperature ranges may require additional model adjustments.
The quantitative improvement depends on the accuracy of defect characterization and the quality of the machine-learning training data.
Scattering parameters are difficult to calibrate for complex defect morphologies.
First-principles simulations are challenging for disordered multi-principal-element alloys.
A prediction error exceeding ±15% at either 150 K or 800 K for a 1 wt.% oxygen specimen will falsify the hypothesis.
